title: {{server}} done right scores 100%
steps: The lab asks {{server}} for a token-less call and reads the 401 challenge.
It follows resource_metadata to the protected resource metadata, then to the authorization server metadata.
On the mock it also runs the token flow, a wrong-audience token and a too-small-scope call.
takeaway: A target that follows the MCP authorization page passes every MUST and SHOULD the lab can test.

title: {{org}}: no protected resource metadata
steps: The 401 still points at a metadata URL, but it answers 404.
Checks that need the document report not tested rather than guessing.
takeaway: Without RFC 9728 metadata a client cannot find the authorization server. The MCP page makes this a MUST.

title: {{org}}: empty first parameter in WWW-Authenticate
steps: The header reads 'Bearer , resource_metadata=...'.
A tolerant parser still finds resource_metadata; a strict one stops at the empty element.
takeaway: One stray comma is invalid auth-param syntax. Which real clients choke on it is UNVERIFIED.

title: {{org}}: plain-http metadata URL
steps: resource_metadata is an http:// URL.
The lab does not fetch it and falls back to the well-known URIs, as the MCP page allows.
takeaway: Metadata that can be rewritten in transit lets an attacker choose the authorization server.

title: {{org}}: S256 not advertised
steps: code_challenge_methods_supported lists only plain.
takeaway: MCP clients must refuse to proceed without S256 advertised; ChatGPT says such servers are unsupported.

title: {{org}}: resource parameter ignored
steps: The authorization server issues a token with a default audience.
An unrelated resource is accepted instead of invalid_target.
takeaway: Tokens must be bound to the MCP server they were requested for (RFC 8707).

title: {{org}}: no issuer identification
steps: authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported is missing and the redirect carries no iss.
takeaway: RFC 9207 closes the authorization server mix-up gap; ChatGPT ties its stable redirect URI to it.

title: {{org}}: wrong shape for insufficient scope
steps: Calling {{writeTool}} with only {{readScope}} gets a bare 403 with no error and no scope.
takeaway: Without error=insufficient_scope and the needed scope, a client cannot step up.

title: {{org}}: open dynamic registration
steps: Anonymous registration accepts an http redirect URI on another host.
Six registrations in a row are all accepted.
takeaway: Open DCR should validate redirect URIs and be gated or throttled. Throttling is a lab heuristic (UNVERIFIED as a requirement).

title: {{org}}: no CIMD support
steps: client_id_metadata_document_supported is absent; registration_endpoint is still offered.
takeaway: CIMD is the MCP page's default for clients with no prior relationship (SHOULD).

title: {{org}}: stale metadata
steps: Metadata is cacheable for a year and advertises a jwks_uri that now answers 404.
takeaway: A lab heuristic (UNVERIFIED as a requirement): stale metadata strands clients on dead endpoints.

title: {{org}}: audience not validated
steps: A token minted for {{sibling}} is accepted by {{server}}.
takeaway: The MCP page makes audience validation a MUST: otherwise tokens can be passed through.

title: A gateway that answers metadata for any path
steps: The lab asks for metadata at a path that cannot exist and still gets 200.
It warns instead of failing: the metadata is valid, but it cannot prove the application is there.
takeaway: A gateway can answer RFC 9728 metadata for any path, so a probe proves the gateway, not the app behind it.

title: {{org}}: no challenge at all
steps: A token-less request is answered 200.
With no 401 and no WWW-Authenticate there is nothing to discover from; challenge checks that need the header are not tested.
takeaway: Authorization is optional in MCP, but a server that claims to be protected must challenge.

title: {{org}}: 401 without a scope hint
steps: The 401 names the metadata URL but not {{readScope}}.
Clients fall back to scopes_supported or guess, and tend to over-request.
takeaway: The MCP page says servers SHOULD put scope in the challenge so clients ask for least privilege.

title: {{org}}: metadata names another resource
steps: The metadata fetched for {{server}} says its resource is a different URL.
RFC 9728 section 3.3: such data MUST NOT be used.
takeaway: A mismatched resource value is how one server could pose as another.

title: {{org}}: authorization server issuer mismatch
steps: authorization_servers says one issuer string; the metadata says the same string plus a trailing slash.
Issuer comparison is exact, so clients reject the metadata.
takeaway: RFC 8414 section 3.3: the issuer must be identical, character for character.

title: DCR versus CIMD: what each server offers
steps: Three mock servers, same checks.
The comparison reads registration_cimd and registration_dcr from each scorecard.
takeaway: Per the MCP page CIMD is preferred, DCR is the backwards-compatible fallback, and pre-registration is a third path.

title: 401, then 403 insufficient_scope, then step-up
steps: {{client}} calls without a token and gets 401 with scope={{readScope}}.
It gets a {{readScope}} token and calls {{writeTool}}: 403 insufficient_scope naming {{writeScope}}.
It re-authorizes with the challenged scope and the call succeeds.
takeaway: The 403 challenge is the step-up instruction. With the wrong-shape 403 the client is stuck.

title: Step-up fails when the 403 has the wrong shape
steps: Same flow as S15, but the 403 carries no scope.
takeaway: That is why the lab scores the 403 shape.

title: Probe mode against a local mock only
steps: A mock is served on a loopback port and probed over real HTTP.
The probe reads discovery only; checks that need a token or would register a client are reported as not tested.
takeaway: Probe mode is read-only and limited to the one URL typed.

title: Probe refuses private addresses and unsafe targets
steps: Every case is refused before any connection is opened.
DNS names are resolved and every answer is checked; a name that resolves to loopback or a private range is refused.
takeaway: The probe is a guarded client, not a way into the network behind the SE's laptop.

title: Probe never follows a redirect to another origin
steps: Two loopback origins are started.
A same-origin redirect is followed; a redirect to the other origin is refused.
takeaway: The allowlist is the origin typed, and redirects do not widen it.
